content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper studies the seriousness of the exposure bias problem in language modeling. Many NLP researchers believe that the fact that an auto-regressive language model (LM) is conditioned on its own prediction at test time whereas it was conditioned only on training data at training time induces exposure biases. In this work, based on the observation that conditioning on even random inputs or model's past history will still generate valid continuations, questions whether exposure bias is a serious problem. 

The first experiment in this paper is based on measuring the distance between the marginal distribution of the model's predicted word at a certain position to the ground truth marginals, where the model is either fed with ground truth prefix or its own predictions. While this metric shows around 10% difference between ground truth prefix and prediction prefix as the length of the generation goes to around 20, the authors argued that there might be multiple causes since the model's prediction prefix might have a different distribution to the ground truth prefix, leading to different marginals.

To separate out the effect, this work considers measuring the distance between conditionals instead of marginals at a certain position, where conditionals are either conditioned on ground truth prefix or language model prefix. However, since in real data we do not get access to the true conditionals (especially when prefix is generated from the model), this work did a synthetic experiment, using an LSTM language model to generate data as the true data distribution, and use other LSTM models to fit. On this synthetic task, 1) the difference in distances either conditioned on ground truth prefix or predicted prefix is within 3%, and 2) scheduled sampling does not help, but seqGAN helps a bit.

Pros:
1. This paper raises a very interesting question of quantifying exposure bias and proposes a metric to quantify the phenomenon of exposure bias.
2. The experiment on the synthetic task is convincing, showing that exposure bias is not a huge issue there.

Cons:
1. In terms of motivation, the observation here is that auto-regressive LMs are able to self-correct, and authors found similar results for transformers. However, as shown by Holtzmann et al 2019, when directly beam search from the LM, it will produce repetitions that would be further reinforced by the model itself. Those two observations seem contradictory.
2. In the synthetic experiment, the data generator is also of an LSTM architecture, so this setting is similar to knowledge distillation where the student and teacher networks have similar structures. It is well established that the data generated from an LSTM LM is biased (smoother and simpler) compared to the data distribution it's trained on. It is thus not very surprising that the distribution of student's samples is similar to the "true" data distribution (teacher's samples), whereas this is not the case in the real world. One way to evaluate this is to repeat the first ("wrong") experiment on this synthetic dataset, and I would expect the measured differences to be also smaller here. Another way would be using a much more powerful generator and a less powerful LM (what if we use transformer LM to generate but use RNN w/o attention to learn?)
3. What does 3% difference in TV/JS mean? It is a token level metric anyway. Would it mean a less than 3% difference in sequence-level metrics such as BLEU? Does it mean 3% wouldn't compound over time steps? I don't think we can draw any conclusions by looking at this number. 

Overall, I think this paper asks a really interesting question, but this paper doesn't provide a convincing answer, and I am still not sure if exposure bias is a serious problem or not. I am inclined to reject this work unless I can get a convincing assessment of the exposure bias problem.

References:
1. Holtzmann et al 2019. The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration. https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751

content.title: Thanks for the review!
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and advice. Before answering the questions, we want to highlight that we add a new evaluation of EB-C with real human as the data model, in Section 5.3. The result agrees very well with our synthetic experiments. It strengthens our claim that on the contrary to popular belief, exposure bias is only a minor problem for MLE-based LM training. We sincerely hope the reviewer will take this new evaluation into consideration.

Q: In terms of motivation, the observation here is that auto-regressive LMs are able to self-correct, and authors found similar results for transformers. However, as shown by Holtzmann et al 2019, when directly beam search from the LM, it will produce repetitions that would be further reinforced by the model itself. Those two observations seem contradictory.

A: Very good question. Now, the repetition behavior would indeed imply exposure bias, if the repetition is triggered mostly by the low-quality model samples. However, that's not the case. The repetition is typically triggered by very common phrases such as "I don't know" or "I'm not sure.". So, we believe the repetition is a different (but also very interesting) problem for MLE training. Moreover, we don't think the self-correction and repetition behavior is really "contradictory". The self-correction is about some extreme case where the model is fed very distorted history, while repetition is about beam-search.

Actually, we like the work you mentioned and believe that different from exposure bias, repetition is indeed a problem that deserves to be addressed (https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04319 (that's not us)).



Q: In the synthetic experiment, the data generator is also of an LSTM architecture, so this setting is similar to knowledge distillation where the student and teacher networks have similar structures. It is well established that the data generated from an LSTM LM is biased (smoother and simpler) compared to the data distribution it's trained on. It is thus not very surprising that the distribution of student's samples is similar to the "true" data distribution (teacher's samples), whereas this is not the case in the real world. One way to evaluate this is to repeat the first ("wrong") experiment on this synthetic dataset, and I would expect the measured differences to be also smaller here. Another way would be using a much more powerful generator and a less powerful LM (what if we use transformer LM to generate but use RNN w/o attention to learn?)

A: Good question. Please see Section 5.3 about our new evaluation in real setting. Going back to the synthetic setting, we have shown that the student model did not fully recover the teacher model in Table 5: The the test-PPL of LSTM-512 is much worse than the Baseline (teacher) model, which is used as the data model. Moreover, the LSTM-32 model has much less capacity (similar to the reviewer's advice) and even worse test-PPL. Both LSTM-512 and LSTM-32 show insignificant rate of EB-C. 


Q:What does 3\% difference in TV/JS mean? It is a token level metric anyway. Would it mean a less than 3\% difference in sequence-level metrics such as BLEU? Does it mean 3\% wouldn't compound over time steps? I don't think we can draw any conclusions by looking at this number. 
A: The TV/JS metric is the most natural choices to measure the difference between distributions. We also defined the greedy decoding metric, which can be directly interpreted as next-word prediction error. Note that the 3\% is the average over different history lengths. The interpretation is that removing training-testing discrepancy only gives insignificant performance gain. In Figure 2, we do observe that EB-C slowly increases as the history length grows, but most NLG applications only require generating relatively short sentences (e.g. machine translation, image caption, dialogue, summarization ). We conclude that within that range, exposure bias only has minimial effect. This is further strengthened by our new evaluation in Section 5.3.

Finally, as discussed in the last part of our paper, the exposure bias problem is not directly linked to generation quality (e.g. BLEU scores), but it could arguably hamper generation (assuming it's serious). We focus on the exposure bias problem itself in this work. 

We thank the reviewer again for the high-quality comments. We're willing to continue the helpful discussion.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper studies whether exposure bias (the fact that a test time, when  a model is making a sequence of predictions, its history is its own predictions, as opposed to during training, in MLE setting, where its history is ground truth predictions) is a real problem for generation systems. The goal is to find a way to really quantify whether there is an issue empirically. The paper presents one result which argues that it is not (by comparing p_model(x | ground truth history) vs p_model(x | predicted history) for a number of datasets and show it is not a problem. It then argues that this is a bad measure (which I somewhat agree with, although it is a deeply intuitive one), and then tries to compare p_gtdistribution(x | predicted history) vs p_model( x | predicted history). This is where the paper loses me. p_gtdistibution makes no sense from the point of view of real data because we just have samples, and assigning probability is the introduction of a model. The paper tries to continue by using a synthesized distribution here (an LSTM) and then somewhat off-handly declares that in this setting exposure bias is small so its not really a problem. 

I'm very torn about this paper. I found it very interesting, but I also don't think using a synthetic distribution makes sense but I do not have any proposals for how operationalize the paper's proposed definition for measuring exposure bias with real data. The issue is that I don't care if its a problem or not of a synthetic distribution, only real world data. As such, the results toward the end of the paper do not seem valid to me but aren't really overstated (because of the writing, its hard to take the result very seriously, and the authors seem to know). 

I am not sure if the ICLR audience would be as generally interested as I was in the paper, so I am tentatively marking weak reject, although if there is other interest among reviewers I would upgrade.

content.title: Thanks for the review!
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and advice. Before answering the questions, we want to highlight that we add a new evaluation of EB-C with real human as the data model, in Section 5.3. The result agrees very well with our synthetic experiments. It strengthens our claim that on the contrary to popular belief, exposure bias is only a minor problem for MLE-based LM training. We sincerely hope the reviewer will take this new evaluation into consideration.

Q: The paper tries to continue by using a synthesized distribution here (an LSTM) and then somewhat off-handly declares that in this setting exposure bias is small so its not really a problem. ... The issue is that I don't care if its a problem or not of a synthetic distribution, only real world data.
A: We understand that the synthetic experiment may be not convincing enough. Please look at our new evaluation in Section 5.3. In this work we provide empirical evidence from different aspects (the self-recovery ability, synthetic/real measurements of EB-C) to argue that exposure bias is only a minor problem. 


Q: I am not sure if the ICLR audience would be as generally interested as I was in the paper, so I am tentatively marking weak reject, although if there is other interest among reviewers I would upgrade.
A: Firstly, as shown by the professor forcing paper ("https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.09038.pdf"), the exposure bias problem is not special for the LM field. It rises in the general case that the model needs to make a sequence of decisions. Therefore, our analysis could also benefit other fields as well.

Coming back to NLG, we list several facts to show recent interest in the exposure bias problem.
(1) At least two papers that focus on the exposure bias problem have been accepted by ICLR 2019: "RelGAN: Relational generative adversarial networks for text generation", "Optimal Completion Distillation for Sequence Learning".
(2) "Bridging the gap between trainingand inference for neural machine translation" claims to alleviate exposure bias for machine translation. It has been selected as the best paper of ACL2019.
These works show continued research efforts to address exposure bias, blindly assuming it is a really serious problem. They will continue to lead the community to over-estimate the seriousness of exposure bias. That's why we feel it important to get a better understanding of this fundamental problem.

We thank the reviewer again for the high-quality comments, and are willing to continue the helpful discussion.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
This paper studies exposure bias in neural language models and proposes a method to quantify it. The method evaluates the discrepancy between the conditional distributions of the next token--given a history---of the data distribution and the model distribution. The authors conclude that exposure bias seems to play a fairly minor role especially for "short generations" (e.g., short sentences). 

This paper studies exposure bias a seemingly important issue which has remained elusive. Exposure bias has fueled research on text GANs (and other non-MLE-based frameworks), as such better understanding it and/or how it affect MLE-trained models is important and could be impactful. I find that this paper makes a step in that direction. If the results are to be believed, the exposure bias problem may in fact not be as important as once thought. This results also goes in the same direction as recent research where the role of exposure bias never seemed to have materialized. Overall, while I think this kind of analysis if worthwhile, I am not sure that the contribution is significant enough to warrant a publication at this venue. 

Detailed comments/suggestions:
- In Section 5.2, the synthetic data is generated using an LSTM LM. Another LSTM LM is then used to fit this data to quantify exposure bias. I am wondering if using this model could change the results since in this case the trained model could indeed recover the generating distribution (i.e., the model is perfect)? If anything, it seems like it could lessen the impact of exposure bias.

- There are methods such as professor forcing (Lamb et al., NIPS'16) aimed at combating the exposure bias and seem to outperform LMs trained using teacher forcing. Could you briefly discuss these and hypothesize as to where their gains come from? This is in contrast with text GANs that---as you point out---may not be better than MLE-trained models. 

- I am a little puzzled by the second paragraph of the Related Works Section (6). If I understand correctly, your claim is that previous work implied that exposure bias may not be a serious problem in MLE training.  As far as I understand, these works do not make such a claim but rather come to the same conclusion as you do (i.e., it's also possible that text GANs simply do not solve the problem well enough). 

- In Table 1, why show the results using transformers since in the sequel you use an LSTM LM (and transformer results are in the appendix).



Minor comments:

- STOA -> SOTA

- In Eq. 5 the position of the parameters of MGD are not the same as in Example 1.

content.title: Thanks for the review!
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and advice. Before answering the questions, we want to highlight that we add a new evaluation of EB-C with real human as the data model, in Section 5.3. The result agrees very well with our synthetic experiments. It strengthens our claim that on the contrary to popular belief, exposure bias is only a minor problem for MLE-based LM training. We sincerely hope the reviewer will take this new evaluation into consideration.

Q: In Section 5.2, the synthetic data is generated using an LSTM LM. Another LSTM LM is then used to fit this data to quantify exposure bias. I am wondering if using this model could change the results since in this case the trained model could indeed recover the generating distribution (i.e., the model is perfect)?
A: Good question, we have shown this is not the case in Table 5: The the test-PPL of LSTM-512 is much worse than the Baseline model, which is used as the data model. Moreover, the LSTM-32 model has less capacity and even worse test-PPL. Both LSTM-512 and LSTM-32 show insignificant rate of EB-C. And finally, we believe our added real-setting evaluation in Section 5.3 makes our claim more convincing.


Q: There are methods such as professor forcing (Lamb et al., NIPS'16) ... Could you briefly discuss these and hypothesize as to where their gains come from? 

A: In this work we restrict ourselves to the discussion of exposure bias itself, whether the formerly proposed methods do indeed give better generation performance is better addressed by works listed in Section 6 (Related works). As discussed in Section 2, the caveat is that it's hard to tell where the improvement actually comes from. It could be normal regularization effect (e.g. dropout). 

As for the professor forcing paper (we now add the citation, thanks), we find that their improvement is only marginal: "On word level Penn Treebank we did not observe any difference between Teacher Forcing and Professor Forcing." Our work provides an explanation for it, that the exposure bias is not a serious problem at all. We think they propose an interesting algorithm, but their motivation is weak (given our work). We believe it will be more productive to study other weakness of MLE training for LMs.


Q:Section 6. ... your claim is that previous work implied that exposure bias may not be a serious problem in MLE training.  As far as I understand, these works do not make such a claim but rather come to the same conclusion as you do. 

A: Again, in this work we restrict ourselves to the discussion of exposure bias itself. There are several possibilities that could lead to the same outcome that text GAN does not improve over MLE (that's why we use the word "imply"):
(1) Exposure bias is not serious at all.
(2) Exposure bias is indeed serious, but text GANs does not solve it well.
(3) Exposure bias is indeed serious, text GANs indeed alleviates it, but it introduces other problems (unstable training of GAN).
So, comparing with the generation performance of text GANs will not help us get a better understanding at what are the weakness of the original MLE training, which is the goal of our work.


Q:  I am not sure that the contribution is significant enough.... 
A: Firstly, as shown by the professor forcing paper, the exposure bias problem is not special for the LM field. It rises in the general case that the model needs to make a sequence of decisions. Therefore, our analysis could also benefit other fields as well.

Coming back to NLG, we list several facts to show recent interest in the exposure bias problem.
(1) At least two papers that claim to address the exposure bias problem have been accepted by ICLR 2019: "RelGAN: Relational generative adversarial networks for text generation", "Optimal Completion Distillation for Sequence Learning".
(2) "Bridging the gap between trainingand inference for neural machine translation" claims to alleviate exposure bias for machine translation. It has been selected as the best paper of ACL2019.
These works show continuing research efforts to address exposure bias, blindly assuming it is a really serious problem. They will continue to lead the community to over-estimate the seriousness of exposure bias. That's why we feel it important to get a better understanding of this fundamental problem.

Q: In Table 1, why show the results using transformers since in the sequel you use an LSTM LM (and transformer results are in the appendix).
A: We provide results for both LSTM and transformer model, with very similar observations. For Table 1, we show the transformer result because it generally has better generation quality, which will help readers to understand our point. 

Minor comments: - STOA -> SOTA - In Eq. 5 the position of the parameters of MGD are not the same as in Example 1.
A: Thanks! We have changed these to be correct.

We thank the reviewer again for the high-quality comments, and are willing to continue the helpful discussion.

Thanks for the response. It mostly makes sense to me and I will think some more about some of its implications. I do have a few follow-up questions. 

- To be clear, are you saying that your work applies to other tasks such as translation? Or are you saying that exposure bias is an important issue and use this ACL'19 paper /prize as an example of work that studies exposure bias albeit for a different task?

content.title: Thanks!
content.comment:
Thanks for continuing the discussion with us.

Q: To be clear, are you saying that your work applies to other tasks such as translation? Or are you saying that exposure bias is an important issue and use this ACL'19 paper /prize as an example of work that studies exposure bias albeit for a different task?
A: Yes, we mean the later case. We list these works to point out that researchers are assuming exposure bias is a serious problem, without actually studying it. Although our work is not about NMT in particular, we do show that the self-recovery phenomena also exists in NMT in Appendix A. So, we believe the existence of exposure bias in NMT is also very dubious. An important point we want to make in this work is that: before we set out to alleviate some problem, we should at least show it's a meaningful problem. Otherwise, valuable research efforts could be wasted.

Q: Regarding the additional experiment. It would be good to provide (at least in an appendix) the full details about the study (exact setup including the question given to the turkers, the number of unique turkers, the number of turkers per question, inter-rater agreement, estimator variance, etc.)
A: Thanks for the suggestion, we now provide more info in Appendix D. Since most turker only do a small number of HITs, we think inter-rater agreement, estimator variance maybe not very informative. But feel free to give us more advice.

Thanks again, and we're willing to continue the helpful discussion.
